messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keanu, a 53-year-old airline pilot with an impeccable twenty-five-year record, had always defined himself by his calm under pressure. That sense of self began to unravel six months ago. During a layover in a country experiencing sudden political upheaval, he was dragged from his hotel room by armed men. For four days, he was held in a windowless, subterranean cell, accused of being a foreign agent. The memories do not play like a film; they surface as a series of stark, still photographs in his mind: the face of another prisoner, eyes wide with terror; the glint of a boot on the concrete floor; the rusted bars of the cell door. When these images arise, he is often overwhelmed by a wave of pure, undifferentiated emotion so powerful he has to physically brace himself, shutting down the memory before it can fully form.

The triggers are insidious and everywhere. Initially, he believed he could manage them, walling off the experience. But the world kept echoing the cell. Walking through the crowded terminals of the airports he once navigated with ease now provokes a visceral sense of danger. Surrounded by the press of bodies, he feels a primal certainty that an attack is imminent, and he finds himself scanning faces, watching hands, profiling strangers as he moves through the concourse, convinced he can spot the threat before it materializes. This constant vigilance has bled into his home life; an unusual silence in the house at night no longer feels peaceful but pregnant with menace, compelling him to get up and check that every door and window is bolted, a ritual he might repeat three or four times before dawn.

The sensory details of the trauma are the most potent ambush. He was recently preparing for a flight when the scent of jet fuel mixed with the damp morning air, and in an instant, he was back in the suffocating darkness of the cell, smelling the stale sweat and damp earth. The memory brought with it not just a photograph but a physical sensation of dread, the same gut-wrenching panic that something terrible was about to happen. This feeling of immediate threat, born from the memory, sent him back through the cockpit pre-flight check three times, his hands shaking as he confirmed the latch on the cockpit door was secure.

Sometimes, the triggers and memories feed each other in a dizzying loop. Last month, a passenger on his flight became belligerent with the cabin crew over a seating issue. Seeing this display of misbehavior, this casual disregard for rules, was enough to ignite Keanu’s hypervigilance. His focus narrowed on the man, his mind screaming that this was how it started—with chaos and a breakdown of order. The intense threat perception, in turn, dredged up a memory: the photographic image of a guard laughing while striking another prisoner. The memory itself then became a new trigger, making him so exquisitely sensitive that the ordinary sound of a baby crying two rows back felt like a physical assault, another harbinger of the suffering he had witnessed.

This cycle has tightened its grip over the months. His constant scanning for threats makes him more likely to notice things that he then interprets as dangerous—a group of teenagers laughing too loudly, a passenger arguing—which then serve as fresh triggers. These triggers bring back the photographic, overwhelming memories, and the memories confirm his belief that the world is a fundamentally unsafe place, which fuels his need to remain on high alert. His wife notes that he has become a ghost in their home, silent and watchful. At work, his co-pilot filed a report after Keanu became fixated on a minor maintenance issue, unable to let it go, delaying their departure by an hour. He was grounded pending a psychological evaluation. It was this formal suspension, this stripping away of the one identity he had left, that finally brought him to therapy. He fears he is permanently broken, and what frightens him most is not the memory of the cell, but the terrifying possibility that he will never again feel safe in the world, or in his own mind.
